lines: {target}? Gentle ground can make travelers careless.
If anyone heads for Meadow, tell them. Rest there, but do not forget night comes.
Flowers and bees do not bar the dark.
Hearing about tall flowers hiding uneven ground makes Meadow sound like a place for careful feet.
I will remember Meadow as soft grass that still needs a lantern.
Every traveler should be able to find the lone tree beside the downhill path without help.
Did you set up a low path down before clouds cover the slope before exploring, or only when it was time to leave?
Something like tall flowers hiding uneven ground can seem ordinary until it puts the whole group at risk.
If flowers, honey, and a gentle place to rest had not been there, would you still have taken the trip?
I trust a nervous flock around the flowered slopes of Meadow more than a confident traveler.
An ordinary day at home beats a high meadow full of flowers and quiet grass any time.
I would keep picturing bees humming while wind moves over the grass for days.
Even a muddy path sounds good after a high meadow full of flowers and quiet grass.
I'd keep a shorter line and use louder voices across the flowered slopes of Meadow.
We could sort food and nerves at a low stone wall above the meadow before facing the flowered slopes of Meadow.
Any sign of a bee defending flowers near the path would end the exploring for me. Everyone goes back together.
Around Meadow, I would watch the last traveler as closely as the leader.
If I ran into bees, hidden holes, and storms rolling over the ridge, I would turn around.
You may keep the adventure around a high meadow full of flowers and quiet grass. I will keep the bread and a roof that does not move.
Around the flowered slopes of Meadow, helping hands matter more than a full pack.
{target}? Stone peaks make every fall honest.
If anyone heads for Stony Peaks, tell them. Bring blocks and stop before your legs shake.
Bare rock gives little cover and no softness.
That tale makes Stony Peaks feel much closer than it did a moment ago.
I will remember Stony Peaks as high stone with hard answers.
I would keep the tale of loose calcite above a steep fall ready for the next traveler.
How did a descent marked before reaching the top help once it was time to turn back?
A careful group plans for the possibility of hard wind over the bare summit before leaving home.
The part about goat calls echoing off empty rock is what I keep picturing.
Before exploring Stony Peaks, I would make sure everyone could point to a broad ledge below the highest ridge.
Your tale from Stony Peaks makes one thing clear. A shepherd counts the flock because one missing life matters. I would do the same there.
No reward keeps me there once goats, loose rock, and sheer drops on every side begins.
The first village roof must have been a welcome sight after bare stone peaks above the cloud line.
Nothing beside our pasture prepares a person for bare stone peaks above the cloud line.
I would match my step to whoever found the bare stone ridges of Stony Peaks hardest.
Careful movement matters more than people think, especially around bare stone peaks above the cloud line.
A watch call should be simple if there are signs of a goat charging near the edge nearby.
The pale calcite trail downhill would be our answer to anyone asking where to regroup.
I can see why you went after emeralds and coal exposed near the summit, but that was a hard road.
Hooves find trouble before eyes sometimes, especially around the bare stone ridges of Stony Peaks.
{target}? Gravel moves when you most need it still.
If anyone heads for Windswept Gravelly Hills, tell them. Test every slope before trusting it.
Loose stone tells lies under boots.
A place like Windswept Gravelly Hills can turn one small mistake into a long walk home.
I will remember Windswept Gravelly Hills as windy hills that slide under pressure.
If the animals balked at the loose gravel slopes of Windswept Gravelly Hills, I would trust them before my pride.
I would leave the treasure and deal with falling gravel, steep drops, and wind across bare ridges.
I would count everyone each time we passed the solid stone line leading down.
The thought of a goat knocking stones down the slope sounds like trouble best met with distance and a headcount.
You found your way home after seeing gravel hills shifting under every careless step. That is the part I like best.
I would divide food by need if gravel sliding toward a steep drop delayed us.
Was finding flint and exposed ore gathered from stable ground truly worth the road you took?
After leaving behind gravel hills shifting under every careless step, even our muddy sheepfold must have looked welcoming.
You described gravel ticking down the slope after each footstep so clearly that I nearly felt I was there.
When it was time to leave, could you still reach a route along grass instead of loose gray ridges?
I would use a stone shelf out of the wind for a headcount before deciding whether to continue.
Going from fences and friendly lanterns to gravel hills shifting under every careless step must have felt like another world.
I would call the whole group in before we tried the loose gravel slopes of Windswept Gravelly Hills.
Torn wool can be mended. Gravel sliding toward a steep drop may not leave the same chance.
A folded blanket would make a hard rest at a stone shelf out of the wind easier.
{target}? Hard wind turns every edge into advice.
If anyone heads for Windswept Hills, tell them. Keep low and do not race the mountain.
Clouds move fast up there and so can mistakes.
Now I understand why a hollow on the sheltered slope mattered so much near Windswept Hills.
I will remember Windswept Hills as high rough land that talks in gusts.
The danger I would plan around is sharp drops beside narrow paths.
Near Windswept Hills, I would rather hear a false alarm than miss a goat charging along the ridge.
Even the far pasture feels close after hearing about high broken hills under a constant crosswind.
We should reach a hollow on the sheltered slope before we have to deal with hard rain and wind over the hilltop.
Home must have looked wonderful once the sight of high broken hills under a constant crosswind was behind you and the village bell was ahead.
A headcount before and after the exposed ridges of Windswept Hills sounds wiser than trusting memory.
A hollow on the sheltered slope would give me somewhere to check feet and share food.
You found your way home after seeing high broken hills under a constant crosswind. That is the part I like best.
The moment I noticed cliffs, goats, and weather arriving without cover, I would start looking for the way out.
The risk from sharp drops beside narrow paths is reason enough to keep the journey unhurried.
No one goes searching alone. We wait together at the lower green ridge toward home.
If coal and a wide view of the surrounding land had not been there, would you still have taken the trip?
Leaving safely sounds harder than arriving. Did a sheltered descent chosen before sunset help when you needed it?
The picture I keep getting is wind roaring over grass and exposed stone.
The flock's mood would guide me before committing anyone to the exposed ridges of Windswept Hills.
